hints: Focus on how the pull on bonding electrons changes as you move left to right across Period 3.
Remember that nuclear charge increases from Na to Cl while shielding stays similar, so electronegativity should rise steadily with no big dips.
Look for the one smooth, continuously rising graph and check that the others show the famous peaks or dips of melting point, radius and ionisation energy.
walkthrough:
**Recall what electronegativity does across a period**

Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract a pair of bonding electrons. Across Period 3 from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Cl}$, proton number increases but electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding hardly changes.

Trend rule:
$$\text{increasing nuclear charge + similar shielding} \rightarrow \text{increasing electronegativity}$$

**Predict the shape of the graph**

This means the graph should rise steadily from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Cl}$, with no sharp peak in the middle and no dip down. It is a smooth, general increase.

**Match the shape and eliminate the others**

Graph A has a huge peak at $\text{Si}$, that is melting point with giant covalent silicon highest. Graph B falls steadily, that is atomic radius decreasing. Graph C goes up and down with dips at $\text{Al}$ and $\text{S}$, that is first ionisation energy. Only one graph shows the smooth steady rise we predicted, and that must be electronegativity.

options.A: Incorrect. Graph A shows a low value for Na, higher for Mg and Al, a very high peak at Si, then a sharp drop for P, S, Cl. This is the melting point trend. Si has a giant covalent lattice with strong covalent bonds, so it has the highest melting point, not the highest electronegativity.
options.B: Incorrect. Graph B shows a steady decrease from Na to Cl. This is the atomic radius trend. Increasing nuclear charge pulls the same shell in more strongly across the period, so atoms get smaller. Electronegativity does the opposite, it increases.
options.C: Incorrect. Graph C rises overall but has two clear dips, one at Al below Mg and one at S below P. This is the classic first ionisation energy pattern due to the $3p$ subshell starting at Al and spin-pair repulsion at S. Electronegativity does not show these dips, it rises smoothly.
options.D: Correct. Graph D shows a smooth, continuous increase from Na (least electronegative) to Cl (most electronegative). This fits the theory perfectly: more protons across the period means a stronger pull on bonding electrons, with little extra shielding, so electronegativity increases steadily.
